name: Microwave hair removal

card.summary: An experimental approach to hair removal that proposes using microwave energy to damage hair follicles for smoother, hairless skin.
card.note: Listed among methods proposed without published clinical proof.

quick.overview:
Microwave hair removal refers to proposed devices that would use microwave energy to disable hair follicles, aiming for smooth, hair-free skin without shaving or waxing.

Wikipedia's hair removal article lists it under "doubtful methods", a section for approaches sold or proposed without published clinical proof that they work as claimed.
quick.how: The concept resembles other energy-based removal such as laser, IPL and diode devices, which target follicles with energy over several sessions. No established consumer protocol for microwave removal is documented.
quick.risks: Hair removal methods in general can cause irritation, minor burns, scarring, ingrown hairs and folliculitis. For this method, no published safety data are available.

lead: Microwave hair removal is an experimental concept in which microwave energy would be directed at hair follicles to stop growth. Wikipedia's hair removal article places it in a "Doubtful methods" list, noting that many methods have been proposed or sold without published clinical proof that they work as claimed.[1]

Established permanent-reduction methods include laser, intense pulsed light and diode epilation, while electrology is the only method the FDA recognizes as permanent.[1] Those energy-based techniques are the context in which microwave approaches are discussed.

angle.text: The idea is a lasting smooth-skin result without repeated shaving or waxing. People interested in laser-style options may look at it as a possible alternative.

paras: Hair removal splits into depilation (surface), epilation (from the root) and permanent reduction.[1] Microwave removal would belong to the last group if it worked as proposed.[1]
Hair removal can cause skin inflammation, minor burns, lesions, scarring, ingrown hairs, bumps and folliculitis.[1]
